For noncompact locally compact Hausdorff X, checked the topology directly: unions and finite intersections of compact-complement neighborhoods remain of that form, using finite unions and closed subsets of compact sets. For compactness, an open cover of X⁺ has a member containing ∞, whose complement is compact; finitely cover that complement and add the ∞-member. For Hausdorffness, separate two X-points in X, and separate x from ∞ by a neighborhood of x with compact closure, whose ∞-neighborhood is its compact-complement. X is open and dense because every nonempty ∞-neighborhood contains X\K and X is noncompact. Coordinator also checked uniqueness: in any compact Hausdorff extension by one point, complements of neighborhoods of that point are compact subsets of X; conversely any compact K in X is closed in the extension, so its complement is such a neighborhood. This determines the topology. Stereographic projection gives the Euclidean examples: y maps to (2y/(1+norm(y)^2),(norm(y)^2-1)/(1+norm(y)^2)); infinity maps to the north pole, and complements of compact sets give continuity there. The real line and complex plane are the n=1 and n=2 cases. If X is compact its complement at infinity is the singleton, which is isolated and prevents density.

entries.evidence: Coordinator checked the full statement in the metric subspace K. Compact implies sequentially compact: if no subsequence converges, each x has a ball containing only finitely many sequence indices (otherwise choose successive indices in radius 1/n balls); a finite subcover contradicts infinitely many indices. Conversely sequential compactness implies total boundedness: failure gives an epsilon-separated sequence, which has no convergent subsequence. Every open cover has a Lebesgue number: otherwise choose x_n with B_K(x_n,1/n) contained in no cover member; a convergent subsequence tends to x, and a member containing a ball B_K(x,r) eventually contains those small balls, contradiction. A finite epsilon-net for epsilon smaller than that Lebesgue number now supplies a finite subcover. No countability of the given open cover is assumed. The restriction to metric spaces is essential.
